This tutorial will cover the Seurat scRNA-seq analysis with the following steps:



 This tutorial will cover the Seurat scRNA-seq analysis with the following steps:

 number of genes/nFeature_RNA

Option-1: standard LogNormalize

After removing unwanted cells (selecting cells you want) from the dataset, the next step is to normalize the data. We need data normalization, because the cell heterogeneity in single-cell RNA-seq data is often confounded by technical variations such as sequencing depth, batch effect. 

By default, Seurat employ a global-scaling normalization method “LogNormalize” that normalizes the feature expression measurements for each cell by the total expression, multiplies this by a scale factor (10,000 by default), and log-transforms the result. In Seurat v5, Normalized values are stored in Seurat.object[["RNA"]]$data. These steps help shift the data into a normal distribution, as opposed to a skewed distribution. 

While LogNormalize method is standard and widely used in scRNA-seq analysis, global-scaling relies on an assumption that each cell originally contains the same number of RNA molecules. 

Option-2: SCTransform

Alternatively, Seurat team have developed workflows for the single cell preprocessing that do not make these above assumptions. This is called SCTransform() normalization workflow. The method is based on the use of analytic Pearson residuals for normalization of single-cell RNA-seq data, which is described in this paper (https://genomebiology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13059-021-02584-9), with a separate vignette using Seurat here (https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/sctransform_vignette). The use of SCTransform replaces the need to run NormalizeData, FindVariableFeatures, or ScaleData. It can also be adjusted by molecular items such as:  

 ---Cell cycle genes: If you suspect that cell cycle effects are a significant source of variation.
 ---Ribosomal genes: If ribosomal content varies greatly between cells.
 ---Mitochondrial Genes contamination


When dealing with datasets have more technical effects, SCTransform performs better than LogNormalize because it strongly removes technical effects from the data. We can select higher PCs are more likely to represent subtle, but biologically relevant, sources of heterogeneity – so including them may improve downstream analysis.Check the details in the tutorial and paper below: 

 https://satijalab.org/seurat/archive/v4.3/sctransform_vignette

 https://genomebiology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13059-021-02584-9


After either option-1 (longNormalize) or option-2 (SCTransform), we need to: 

6. Perform linear dimensional reduction

Next we perform PCA on the scaled data. By default, only the previously determined variable features are used as input. 

Seurat provides several useful ways of visualizing both cells and features that define the PCA, including VizDimReduction(), DimPlot(), and DimHeatmap(). 

However, this quantitative approach using Elbow plot is working very well determine the ideal PCs needed for downstream analysis. 
https://hbctraining.github.io/scRNA-seq/lessons/elbow_plot_metric.html

In brief, based on ElbowPlot(object, ndims = 40) plot, we could roughly determine the majority of the variation by where the elbow occurs (touches the ground). While this gives us a good rough idea of the number of PCs needed to be included, a more quantitative approach may be a bit more reliable. We can calculate where the principal components start to elbow by taking the larger (should be smaller?) value of:

(1) The point where the principal components only contribute 5% of standard deviation and the principal components cumulatively contribute 90% of the standard deviation.
(2) The point where the percent change in variation between the consecutive PCs is less than 0.1%.



7. Cluster the cells

Seurat first construct a K-nearest neighbor (KNN) graph based on the euclidean distance in PCA space, and refine the edge weights between any two cells based on the shared overlap in their local neighborhoods (Jaccard similarity). This step is performed using the FindNeighbors() function, and takes as input the previously defined dimensionality of the dataset (i.e., first 20 PCs).

To cluster the cells, Seurat next apply modularity optimization techniques such as the Louvain algorithm (default) or SLM [SLM, Blondel et al., Journal of Statistical Mechanics], to iteratively group cells together, with the goal of optimizing the standard modularity function. The FindClusters() function implements this procedure, and contains a resolution parameter that sets the ‘granularity’ of the downstream clustering, with increased values leading to a greater number of clusters. We find that setting this parameter between 0.4-1.2 typically returns good results for single-cell datasets of around 3K cells. Optimal resolution often increases for larger datasets. The clusters can be found using the Idents() function.

Student will test low, medium, and high resolution, and choose an appropriate resolution that fit biological expectations. 


8. Run non-linear dimensional reduction (UMAP/tSNE)

Seurat offers several non-linear dimensional reduction techniques, such as tSNE and UMAP, to visualize and explore these datasets. The goal of these algorithms is to learn underlying structure in the dataset, in order to place similar cells together in low-dimensional space. Therefore, cells that are grouped together within graph-based clusters determined above should co-localize on these dimension reduction plots.

```{r}
# Install all packages (This part can be done by TA ahead of class)


#Seurat 5: Install from CRAN

install.packages('Seurat')

library(Seurat)

# Seurat does not require, but makes use of, packages developed by other labs that can substantially enhance speed and performance. These include presto (Korunsky/Raychaudhari labs), BPCells (Greenleaf Lab), and glmGamPoi (Huber Lab). We recommend users install these along with Seurat:

setRepositories(ind = 1:3, addURLs = c('https://satijalab.r-universe.dev', 'https://bnprks.r-universe.dev/'))
install.packages(c("BPCells", "presto", "glmGamPoi"))


# Seurat also recommend installing these additional packages, which are used in our vignettes, and enhance the functionality of Seurat:
# SeuratData: automatically load datasets pre-packaged as Seurat objects
# SeuratWrappers: enables use of additional integration and differential expression methods
# Install the remotes package

if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("remotes")
}
remotes::install_github("satijalab/seurat-data", quiet = TRUE)
remotes::install_github("satijalab/seurat-wrappers", quiet = TRUE)

library(SeuratData)
library(SeuratWrappers)


## Harmony is an algorithm for performing integration of single cell genomics datasets

install.packages("harmony")

library("harmony")

## FastMNN Integration is a method in the Seurat v5 package that integrates cells
# Haghverdi L, Lun ATL, Morgan MD, Marioni JC (2018). “Batch effects in single-cell RNA-sequencing data are corrected by matching mutual nearest neighbors.” Nat. Biotechnol., 36(5), 421–427. doi:10.1038/nbt.4091.
# It's a Single-Cell Batch Correction Methods. This includes methods based on detecting mutually nearest neighbors, as well as several efficient variants of linear regression of the log-expression values. Functions are also provided to perform global rescaling to remove differences in depth between batches, and to perform a principal components analysis that is robust to differences in the numbers of cells across batches.

# To install this package, start R (version "4.4") and enter:

if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("batchelor")

library("batchelor")


```

```{r}

library(Seurat)

library("harmony")

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

options(future.globals.maxSize = 1e9) 

# the options() function is used to set or get global options that affect the way R computes and displays information. These options can control various aspects of R's behavior and the settings of different packages.
# future.globals.maxSize is an option used by the future package in R, which is utilized in conjunction with the Seurat package for parallel processing. Setting future.globals.maxSize to 1e9 (one billion) means that the maximum allowed size for globals (i.e., data and objects) that can be exported to each parallel worker is set to one billion bytes (or one gigabyte). This helps to control the memory usage when performing parallel computations to prevent overloading the system with too large data transfers.
```

# 4. merge all samples into one object (obj) for integrated analysis


```{r}
Control_vs_FCP1.merge <- merge(x= Control.1, y=list(Control.2, FCP1.1, FCP1.2))

View(Control_vs_FCP1.merge@meta.data)


```


# 5. Perform analysis without integration


```{r}
# We can first analyze the dataset without integration. The resulting clusters are defined both by cell type and treatment condition, which may create challenges for downstream analysis.

# Option-1 
# run standard LogNormalization anlaysis workflow
Control_vs_FCP1 <- NormalizeData(Control_vs_FCP1.merge)
Control_vs_FCP1 <- FindVariableFeatures(Control_vs_FCP1)
Control_vs_FCP1 <- ScaleData(Control_vs_FCP1)


# Option-2 
# we can also perform integration using SCTransform-normalized data as we did for individual dataset.

# options(future.globals.maxSize = 3e+09)
# Control_vs_FCP1 <- SCTransform(Control_vs_FCP1)

###

```


# 6. Perform linear dimensional reduction


```{r}

# RunPCA

Control_vs_FCP1 <- RunPCA(Control_vs_FCP1)

# Determine the ‘dimensionality’ of the dataset


## We will use a quantitative approach based on Elbow plot: a ranking of principle components based on the percentage of variance explained by each one (ElbowPlot() function). 
## https://hbctraining.github.io/scRNA-seq/lessons/elbow_plot_metric.html

## We first display the firt 50 PCs on the ElbowPlot. 

ElbowPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, ndims = 50)

## Based on ElbowPlot(object, ndims = 50) plot, we could roughly determine the majority of the variation by where the elbow occurs (touches the ground). While this gives us a good rough idea of the number of PCs needed to be included, a more quantitative approach may be a bit more reliable. We can calculate where the principal components start to elbow by taking the larger (should be smaller?) value of:

## (1) The point where the principal components only contribute 5% of standard deviation and the principal components cumulatively contribute 90% of the standard deviation.
## (2) The point where the percent change in variation between the consecutive PCs is less than 0.1%.

## We will start by calculating the first metric:
# Determine percent of variation associated with each PC
pct <- Control_vs_FCP1[["pca"]]@stdev / sum(Control_vs_FCP1[["pca"]]@stdev) * 100

# Calculate cumulative percents for each PC
cumu <- cumsum(pct)

# Determine which PC exhibits cumulative percent greater than 90% and % variation associated with the PC as less than 5
co1 <- which(cumu > 90 & pct < 5)[1]

co1

## [1] result will be displayed (i.e. 43)

## The first metric returns PC (i.e. 43) as the PC matching these requirements. Let’s check the second metric, which identifies the PC where the percent change in variation between consecutive PCs is less than 0.1%:

# Determine the difference between variation of PC and subsequent PC
co2 <- sort(which((pct[1:length(pct) - 1] - pct[2:length(pct)]) > 0.1), decreasing = T)[1] + 1

# last point where change of % of variation is more than 0.1%.
co2

## [1]  result will be displayed (i.e. 17)

## This second metric returns PC (i.e. 17). Usually, we would choose the minimum of these two metrics as the PCs covering the majority of the variation in the data.

# Minimum of the two calculation
pcs <- min(co1, co2)

pcs

# 17

```



# 7. Cluster the cells


```{r}
# Cluster the cell. 

Control_vs_FCP1 <- FindNeighbors(Control_vs_FCP1, dims = 1:pcs, reduction = "pca")


Control_vs_FCP1 <- FindClusters(Control_vs_FCP1, resolution = 1, cluster.name = "unintegrated_clusters")

```


# 8. Run non-linear dimensional reduction (UMAP/tSNE)


```{r}
# using UMAP (Most popular)

Control_vs_FCP1 <- RunUMAP(Control_vs_FCP1, dims = 1:pcs, reduction = "pca", reduction.name = "umap.unintegrated")

## View metadata to see the data information. 
## origin.ident
## nCount_RNA
## nFeature_RNA
## source
## unintegrated_clusters
## seurat_clusters

View (Control_vs_FCP1@meta.data)


## Visualize our cell clusters. 

p1 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", label = TRUE, pt.size = 1, label.size = 8)

p2 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", group.by = "orig.ident", pt.size = 1)

p3 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", group.by = "source", pt.size = 1)


p1 + p2 + p3


## It seems even without integration, our batch effect is small, which is good! 

### Other visualization tools. 
### split the UMAPs by samples 

DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", split.by = "orig.ident", pt.size = 1.5, label = TRUE, label.size = 8)

### split the UMAPs by treatments 


DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", split.by = "source", pt.size = 1.5, label = TRUE, label.size = 8)


```

```{r}
# Now let's try one by one, and then compare the cluster results.

# CCAIntegration

Control_vs_FCP1 <- IntegrateLayers(
  object = Control_vs_FCP1, method = CCAIntegration,
  orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "integrated.cca",
  verbose = FALSE
)


# Cluster the cell. 

Control_vs_FCP1 <- FindNeighbors(Control_vs_FCP1, dims = 1:pcs, reduction = "integrated.cca")

Control_vs_FCP1 <- FindClusters(Control_vs_FCP1, resolution = 1, cluster.name = "cca_clusters")

# Run non-linear dimensional reduction (UMAP/tSNE)
# using UMAP (Most popular)

Control_vs_FCP1 <- RunUMAP(Control_vs_FCP1, dims = 1:pcs, reduction = "integrated.cca", reduction.name = "umap.cca")

## View metadata to see the data information. 
## origin.ident
## nCount_RNA
## nFeature_RNA
## source
## unintegrated_clusters
## seurat_clusters
## cca_clusters

View (Control_vs_FCP1@meta.data)


## Visualize our cell clusters. 


p4 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.cca", label = TRUE, pt.size = 1, label.size = 8)

p5 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.cca", group.by = "orig.ident", pt.size = 1)

p6 <- DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.cca", group.by = "source", pt.size = 1)


p4 + p5 + p6

### split the UMAPs by samples 

DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.cca", split.by = "orig.ident", pt.size = 1.5, label = TRUE, label.size = 8)

### split the UMAPs by treatments 


DimPlot(Control_vs_FCP1, reduction = "umap.cca", split.by = "source", pt.size = 1.5, label = TRUE, label.size = 8)


```

# 11. Finding differentially expressed features/genes between Control and FCP1 treatment in different cell types. 


```{r}

# Once integrative analysis is complete, you can rejoin the layers - which collapses the individual datasets together and recreates the original counts and data layers. You will need to do this before performing any differential expression analysis. However, you can always resplit the layers in case you would like to reperform integrative analysis.

# assign a new object name so it won't change the original one. 

Control_vs_FCP1_deg <- Control_vs_FCP1



## Without Joinlayers, we still have individual dataset in RNA/layers, run the code below: 

Layers(Control_vs_FCP1_deg[["RNA"]])

# [1] "counts.Control.1" "counts.Control.2" "counts.FCP1.1"    "counts.FCP1.2"    "data.Control.1"  
# [6] "data.Control.2"   "data.FCP1.1"      "data.FCP1.2"      "scale.data" 




# rejoin the layers

Control_vs_FCP1_deg <- JoinLayers(Control_vs_FCP1_deg)



# after Joinlayers, we only have in RNA/layers, run the code below: 

Layers(Control_vs_FCP1_deg[["RNA"]])

# [1] "data"       "counts"     "scale.data"



## Find DEG for certain cluster between the two conditions (Control vs FCP1 treatment). 

# Specify the reduction method
reduction_method <- "umap.cca"

# Set the identity class to use 'cca_clusters' and assign to new object
Control_vs_FCP1_deg <- SetIdent(Control_vs_FCP1_deg, value = "cca_clusters")

# Combine cluster identities with treatment information
Control_vs_FCP1_deg$cluster_treatment <- paste(Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg), Control_vs_FCP1_deg$source, sep = "_")

# Set the new identity class
Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg) <- "cluster_treatment"

# Identify DEGs between Control and FCP1 within cluster 13 (change cluster number for whichever you would like to compare) using normalized data
degs_control_vs_fcp1_cluster13 <- FindMarkers(
  object = Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
  ident.1 = "13_Control",  # Cluster 13, Control condition
  ident.2 = "13_FCP1",  # Cluster 13, FCP1 condition
  assay = "RNA",  # Assay used for differential expression
  logfc.threshold = 0.25,  # Log fold-change threshold
  test.use = "wilcox",  # Statistical test to use
  verbose = FALSE
)

# View the top differentially expressed genes
head(degs_control_vs_fcp1_cluster13, n = 15)

# Generate the filename dynamically based on the reduction method
filename <- paste0("DEGs_cluster13_Control_vs_FCP1_", reduction_method, ".xls")

# Export the DEGs to a tab-separated text file
write.table(degs_control_vs_fcp1_cluster13, file = filename, sep = "\t", row.names = TRUE, col.names = NA, quote = FALSE)


```

```{r}
# Check gene of interests if differentially expressed in certain cell type/cluster between the Control and FCP1-1 treatment. 

# Check whether genes of interest are differentially expressed
# between Control and FCP1-1 in Cluster 15

library(Seurat)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Define genes of interest
genes <- c("GRMZM2G173429", "GRMZM5G805026")

# Define cluster of interest
cluster_of_interest <- "15"

# Extract metadata
meta <- FetchData(
  Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
  vars = c("cca_clusters", "source")
)

# Convert metadata columns to factors
meta$cca_clusters <- as.factor(meta$cca_clusters)
meta$source <- as.factor(meta$source)

# Add cell names as a column
meta$cell <- rownames(meta)

# Extract the log-normalized RNA expression matrix
expr_matrix <- GetAssayData(
  Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
  assay = "RNA",
  layer = "data"
)

# Check whether all genes are present
missing_genes <- setdiff(genes, rownames(expr_matrix))

if (length(missing_genes) > 0) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "These genes were not found:",
      paste(missing_genes, collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}

# Extract expression values for the genes of interest
expr <- expr_matrix[genes, , drop = FALSE]

# Transpose so that rows are cells and columns are genes
expr_df <- as.data.frame(t(as.matrix(expr)))

# Add cell names
expr_df$cell <- rownames(expr_df)

# Merge expression data with metadata
expr_df <- merge(
  expr_df,
  meta,
  by = "cell"
)

# Filter for the cluster of interest
expr_df <- expr_df %>%
  filter(cca_clusters == cluster_of_interest)

# Remove unused factor levels
expr_df$source <- droplevels(as.factor(expr_df$source))

# Convert expression data to long format
long_data <- expr_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(genes),
    names_to = "gene",
    values_to = "expression"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(expression),
    !is.na(source)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    gene = factor(gene, levels = genes),
    source = droplevels(as.factor(source))
  )

# Check the number of cells for each gene and source
print(table(long_data$gene, long_data$source))

# Check that exactly two source groups are present
source_groups <- levels(long_data$source)

if (length(source_groups) != 2) {
  stop(
    paste(
      "The source column must contain exactly two groups.",
      "Detected groups:",
      paste(source_groups, collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}

group1_name <- source_groups[1]
group2_name <- source_groups[2]

# Run Wilcoxon rank-sum test separately for each gene
stat_test <- long_data %>%
  group_by(gene) %>%
  summarise(
    group1 = group1_name,
    group2 = group2_name,

    n1 = sum(source == group1_name),
    n2 = sum(source == group2_name),

    mean_group1 = mean(
      expression[source == group1_name],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    mean_group2 = mean(
      expression[source == group2_name],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    median_group1 = median(
      expression[source == group1_name],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    median_group2 = median(
      expression[source == group2_name],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    p = wilcox.test(
      expression[source == group1_name],
      expression[source == group2_name],
      exact = FALSE
    )$p.value,

    data_max = max(expression, na.rm = TRUE),

    data_range = diff(range(expression, na.rm = TRUE)),

    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Adjust p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method
stat_test$p.adj <- p.adjust(
  stat_test$p,
  method = "BH"
)

# Create significance labels
stat_test <- stat_test %>%
  mutate(
    p.adj.signif = case_when(
      p.adj <= 0.0001 ~ "****",
      p.adj <= 0.001  ~ "***",
      p.adj <= 0.01   ~ "**",
      p.adj <= 0.05   ~ "*",
      TRUE            ~ "ns"
    ),

    p.adj.label = paste0(
      "BH-adjusted p = ",
      format.pval(
        p.adj,
        digits = 3,
        eps = 1e-300
      )
    ),

    # Position of horizontal significance line
    y_line = data_max +
      0.10 * ifelse(data_range == 0, 1, data_range),

    # Position of p-value label
    y_label = data_max +
      0.20 * ifelse(data_range == 0, 1, data_range)
  )

# Print statistical results
print(stat_test)

# Save results if desired
write.csv(
  stat_test,
  file = paste0(
    "Cluster_",
    cluster_of_interest,
    "_gene_expression_Wilcoxon_results.csv"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Plot expression and manually add adjusted p-values
expression_plot <- ggplot(
  long_data,
  aes(
    x = source,
    y = expression,
    fill = source
  )
) +
  geom_violin(
    trim = FALSE,
    scale = "width"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.15,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +

  # Add horizontal comparison line
  geom_segment(
    data = stat_test,
    aes(
      x = 1,
      xend = 2,
      y = y_line,
      yend = y_line
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +

  # Add left vertical end of comparison line
  geom_segment(
    data = stat_test,
    aes(
      x = 1,
      xend = 1,
      y = y_line,
      yend = y_line - 0.03 *
        ifelse(data_range == 0, 1, data_range)
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +

  # Add right vertical end of comparison line
  geom_segment(
    data = stat_test,
    aes(
      x = 2,
      xend = 2,
      y = y_line,
      yend = y_line - 0.03 *
        ifelse(data_range == 0, 1, data_range)
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +

  # Add adjusted p-value text
  geom_text(
    data = stat_test,
    aes(
      x = 1.5,
      y = y_label,
      label = p.adj.label
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3.5
  ) +

  facet_wrap(
    ~gene,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +

  # Add extra vertical space for the p-value labels
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0.05, 0.30)
    )
  ) +

  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Gene Expression in Cluster ",
      cluster_of_interest
    ),
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Wilcoxon rank-sum test; ",
      "Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p-values"
    ),
    x = "Source",
    y = "Log-normalized expression",
    fill = "Source"
  ) +

  theme_minimal() +

  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    legend.position = "right",
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    )
  )

# Display plot
print(expression_plot)

# Save plot
ggsave(
  filename = paste0(
    "Cluster_",
    cluster_of_interest,
    "_gene_expression_violin_plot.pdf"
  ),
  plot = expression_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5
)

```



# 12. Finding features/genes enriched in different cell types. 



```{r}
## Export cell type markers for certain cluster with certain integration method. 

library(Seurat)

# Join split RNA layers
Control_vs_FCP1_deg <- JoinLayers(
    object = Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
    assay = "RNA"
)

# Set cluster identities
Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg) <- "cca_clusters"

# Identify enriched markers in cluster 11
# Cluster 11 is compared with all other clusters
cluster11_markers <- FindMarkers(
    object = Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
    ident.1 = "11",
    ident.2 = NULL,
    assay = "RNA",
    slot = "data",
    test.use = "wilcox",
    logfc.threshold = 0.25,
    min.pct = 0.10,
    only.pos = TRUE
)

# Add gene names as a column
cluster11_markers$gene <- rownames(cluster11_markers)

# Move gene column to the beginning
cluster11_markers <- cluster11_markers[
    ,
    c(
        "gene",
        setdiff(colnames(cluster11_markers), "gene")
    )
]

# Sort by adjusted p-value
cluster11_markers <- cluster11_markers[
    order(cluster11_markers$p_val_adj),
]

# View top enriched markers
head(cluster11_markers, 20)

# Export enriched markers as CSV
write.csv(
    cluster11_markers,
    file = "Cluster11_Enriched_Markers_cca.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
)

```

```{r}

## Export cell type markers for certain cluster with certain integration method. 


library(Seurat)

# Join split RNA layers before differential-expression analysis
Control_vs_FCP1_deg <- JoinLayers(
  object = Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
  assay = "RNA"
)

# Set active identities to cca clusters
Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg) <- "cca_clusters"

# Check cluster identities and cell numbers
print(levels(Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg)))
print(table(Idents(Control_vs_FCP1_deg)))

# Identify enriched markers for every cluster
all_cluster_markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  object = Control_vs_FCP1_deg,
  assay = "RNA",
  slot = "data",
  test.use = "wilcox",
  only.pos = TRUE,
  logfc.threshold = 0.25,
  min.pct = 0.10,
  return.thresh = 0.05
)

# Identify the fold-change column used by your Seurat version
logfc_col <- if ("avg_log2FC" %in% colnames(all_cluster_markers)) {
  "avg_log2FC"
} else if ("avg_logFC" %in% colnames(all_cluster_markers)) {
  "avg_logFC"
} else {
  stop("Could not find the average log-fold-change column.")
}

# Add gene names as an explicit column if necessary
if (!"gene" %in% colnames(all_cluster_markers)) {
  all_cluster_markers$gene <- rownames(all_cluster_markers)
}

# Reorder columns so gene and cluster appear first
all_cluster_markers <- all_cluster_markers[
  ,
  c(
    "gene",
    "cluster",
    setdiff(
      colnames(all_cluster_markers),
      c("gene", "cluster")
    )
  )
]

# Sort first by cluster, then adjusted p-value,
# then by decreasing fold change
all_cluster_markers <- all_cluster_markers[
  order(
    as.character(all_cluster_markers$cluster),
    all_cluster_markers$p_val_adj,
    -all_cluster_markers[[logfc_col]]
  ),
]

# View marker counts for each cluster
print(table(all_cluster_markers$cluster))

# View the first rows
head(all_cluster_markers, 20)

# Export all enriched markers for all clusters into one CSV file
write.csv(
  all_cluster_markers,
  file = "All_Clusters_Enriched_Markers_cca.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

message(
  "Exported ",
  nrow(all_cluster_markers),
  " enriched markers to All_Clusters_Enriched_Markers_cca.csv"
)


```
